## Nobody builds the portfolio {.hook background-color="#FAF7F2"}

Last session we constructed the optimal international portfolio: six markets,
specific weights, a Sharpe ratio that beat every country on its own.

::: incremental
-   Almost no household does any of that. They **buy** a portfolio someone else
    assembled — around **$13 trillion** of it, in US mutual funds alone.
-   Which replaces one question with another: the fund charges a fee and makes
    the choices. What exactly is it selling you?
-   Today is the institutions themselves — what they do, what they charge for,
    and why they exist at all.
:::

::: notes
This is the bridge from last session, so make the bridge explicit rather than
starting a new topic cold.

Remind them what they built: the optimal international portfolio, six markets
out of twelve, a Sharpe ratio of 0.179 against 0.160 for the US alone.

*[reveal the first bullet]*

Then the deflating fact. Essentially nobody constructs that themselves. They buy
a fund. Thirteen trillion dollars sits in American mutual funds and the people
who own it did not choose a single holding.

*[ask]* Is that irrational?

No - and that is the point of the whole session. Doing it yourself means
transaction costs, information costs, and a portfolio too small to diversify.
The fund exists because those costs are real.

*[reveal the second and third bullets]*

But the fund charges for solving them, and the manager, not the investor, makes
the choices. Every institution in this chapter is the same bargain in a
different form: it solves a real problem, it takes a fee, and it introduces a
conflict. Tell them to watch for that pattern - it is what section seven is
about, and it is the spine of the session.
:::

# 2 · Mutual funds {.divider .center background-color="#06302F"}

## 2 · The mutual fund: definition and structure

A mutual fund **pools the resources of many small investors** by selling them
shares and using the proceeds to buy securities.

:::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
**Five benefits**, each corresponding to a cost the investor would otherwise
bear:

-   **Liquidity** intermediation — investments convert to cash
-   **Denomination** intermediation — participate in offerings that individually
    require more capital than you have
-   **Diversification**
-   **Cost advantages** — negotiated transaction fees
-   **Managerial expertise**
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
**Structure.** Investors are the shareholders. A **board of directors** oversees
the fund, hires the investment advisor and the underwriter, and in principle can
dismiss the manager and appoint anyone it chooses.
:::
::::

::: {.source}
The board of directors is the subject of the Muñoz (2020) reading in the next
section.
:::

::: notes
Start from the definition, then immediately turn it into the five benefits,
because the definition on its own is inert.

*[the five benefits - do not read them as a list]*

Pair each one with what it would cost the investor alone. Liquidity: you can get
out on a Tuesday. Denomination: a bond issue with a hundred thousand minimum is
simply closed to you otherwise. Diversification: the thing we spent last session
constructing. Cost: the fund trades in size and pays less per trade.
Expertise: someone whose job this is.

*[ask]* Which of those five could you replicate on your own, with enough money?

All of them except denomination - and that is the honest answer. Most of what a
fund sells is a solution to being small.

*[the structure, and point at the source line]*

Flag the board now and tell them to remember it. Investors are shareholders; a
board oversees; the board hires and can fire the advisor. That is the formal
position. Whether it works that way is exactly what they are reading for next
week.
:::

## 2 · Closed-end and open-end

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Closed-end.** A fixed number of **non-redeemable** shares, sold at an initial
offering and then traded over the counter.

The price is set by **supply and demand** — so it can diverge from the value of
the holdings, trading at a premium or a discount.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Open-end.** Investors buy or redeem **at any point**, at the net asset value.

The price is **computed**, not bid. The fund issues and retires shares on
demand, so the share count moves rather than the price.
:::
::::

::: keyidea
Only the **closed-end** price can diverge from net asset value, because only the
closed-end price is set by a market rather than by arithmetic.
:::

::: notes
This distinction is examinable and it is the one they mix up, so spend the three
minutes.

The whole difference is where the price comes from.

Open-end: the fund works out what it owns, divides by the shares, and that is
the price. Supply and demand never enter. If you want in, the fund makes a new
share; if you want out, it retires yours.

Closed-end: a fixed pool of shares traded between investors, like any other
share. The price is whatever someone will pay.

*[ask]* So which of the two can trade below the value of what it owns?

Only the closed-end one - and empirically they very often do, which is a
longstanding puzzle. If a fund holding a hundred of assets trades at ninety,
why does nobody buy it and liquidate it? Leave the question open; it is a good
one and the chapter does not answer it.
:::

## 2 · The four classes, by assets

| Class | Assets | Share |
|:------------------|-------------:|------:|
| Equity | $5.9 trillion | 45% |
| Bond | $3.4 trillion | 26% |
| Money market | $2.7 trillion | 21% |
| Hybrid | $1.0 trillion | 8% |

::: {.smaller}
**Index funds** sit outside this classification: they hold the stocks of the
index being mimicked, giving the benefits of a mutual fund without paying for an
active manager.
:::

::: notes
*[cuttable - the four numbers matter, the sub-classes do not]*

Do not read the table. Make two points from it and move.

Equity is the largest at forty-five percent, which is what you would expect.
Money market funds at twenty-one percent is the number worth pausing on, because
most people think of those as a bank account.

*[on index funds - this is the part to keep if you cut the rest]*

Index funds are the direct application of last session. If the gain comes from
holding the market rather than from picking within it, you do not need a manager
and you should not pay for one. The entire active-versus-passive argument is one
sentence long and they have already done the analysis behind it.

*[ask]* After last session, which would you buy?
:::

## 2 · Composition of the classes

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Stock funds

**Capital appreciation** — rapid share-price growth, unconcerned with dividends.

**Total return** — a balance of income and appreciation.

**World equity** — primarily foreign firms.

Plus **value**, **growth** and **sector** funds.

### Bond funds

**Strategic income** — US corporate bonds, high current income; 42% of bond fund
assets.

**Government** — Treasury, state and local.

**World bond** funds.

Shares of bond fund assets: corporate 15% · national municipal 12% · world 9% ·
government 9% · high yield 8% · state municipal 5%.

### Hybrid and money market

**Hybrid.** Stocks and bonds in one fund; about 5% of all mutual fund accounts.

**Money market mutual funds.** Open-end, holding money market securities only,
usually with check-writing privileges. Higher returns than bank deposits —
and **not federally insured**.

Assets: repos 33% · agency issues 26.7% · Treasury bills 25.6% · other US
securities 12.6%.

:::

::: notes
*[cuttable - if time is short, open only the third tab]*

Three tabs, and only the third contains something they must leave with.

*[tabs one and two]*

Name the categories, do not drill the percentages. The only thing to say is that
the names describe an objective, not a legal category - a fund called "growth"
is making a promise about style, not accepting a constraint.

*[tab three, and slow down here]*

Money market funds. Open-end, short paper, cheque book. They look exactly like a
bank account and they are not one: no federal insurance.

*[ask]* So why does anyone hold one?

Higher yield. And then the obvious follow-up: what happens when a money market
fund's assets fall below a dollar a share? It happened in 2008, it was called
breaking the buck, and it caused a run - on something most holders believed was
a deposit. That is the one fact from this slide worth examining them on.
:::

## 2 · Net asset value

$$\text{NAV} = \frac{\text{stocks} + \text{bonds} + \text{cash} + \text{other assets} - \text{liabilities}}{\text{shares outstanding}}$$

::: ask
A fund holds **$35 million** of stocks, **$15 million** of bonds and
**$3 million** of cash. It has liabilities of **$0.8 million** and
**15 million** shares outstanding.

1.  What is the net asset value per share?
2.  What are those liabilities, in a fund that holds only securities?
3.  If this were a **closed-end** fund, would it trade at that price?
:::

::: notes
Two minutes on their own, then take it.

*[part one]*

Assets: thirty-five plus fifteen plus three, fifty-three million. Less
liabilities of eight hundred thousand, fifty-two point two. Divided by fifteen
million shares.

Three dollars and forty-eight cents.

*[part two - this is the part they skip]*

Ask it before you answer it. A fund holds securities; what can it possibly owe?

Accrued but unpaid management fees, mostly, plus pending settlements. It is a
small number and dropping it gives three dollars fifty-three - five cents, which
sounds trivial until you multiply by fifteen million shares. Seven hundred and
fifty thousand dollars of someone's money.

*[part three - the callback]*

No. The NAV is what it is worth; the closed-end price is what someone will pay.
Those are different numbers and the gap is the puzzle from two slides ago.

**Worked.** 35 + 15 + 3 = 53; less 0.8 = 52.2; divided by 15 = $3.48 per share.
Liabilities are mostly accrued management fees. Dropping them gives 3.53.
:::

## 2 · Hedge funds

:::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
**How they differ from mutual funds**

-   High minimum investment, averaging around **$1 million**
-   A long-term commitment is required
-   High fees — typically **1% of assets plus 20% of profits**
-   Highly **levered**
-   Very little regulation
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
**Strategy.** Exploit unusual spreads between the prices of similar securities —
two things that should trade together and do not.

**Since 2006.** The SEC requires hedge fund advisors to register, prompted by
fraud concerns, and hedge funds reached the average investor through
"retailization".
:::
::::

::: notes
Keep this short and resist the glamour.

The five differences are all one difference: hedge funds are sold to people the
regulator assumes can look after themselves, so the rules are lighter and the
fees are higher.

*[on the fee]*

One and twenty. Say what that means in money: on a hundred million, a million a
year regardless of performance, plus a fifth of any gain. Then the asymmetry
worth naming - the manager takes twenty percent of the upside and none of the
downside, which is an option, and options are worth more when things are
volatile. That is a structural reason to expect risk-taking, quite apart from
anybody's character.

*[on the strategy]*

Convergence trading. Two securities that should trade together have drifted
apart, so you buy one and sell the other and wait. Note what it needs to work:
leverage, because the spreads are small, and time, because convergence can take
longer than your funding lasts. That is Long-Term Capital Management in two
sentences, if anyone asks.
:::

# 3 · Reading discussion {.divider .center background-color="#06302F"}

## Who is watching the manager? {.hook background-color="#FAF7F2"}

A mutual fund's board hires the investment advisor, sets its fee, and can
dismiss it.

::: incremental
-   The advisor is usually the firm that **created the fund** in the first place.
-   So the body that polices the manager was, in most cases, appointed by the
    manager. Does the board's **size** or its **independence** change what the
    fund actually does?
:::

::: notes
Open the discussion with the structure, not with the paper.

Restate the formal position from the first mutual funds slide: investors are
shareholders, a board oversees, the board hires and can fire the advisor.

*[reveal the first bullet]*

Now the awkward fact. The advisor is typically the management company that
founded the fund and assembled the board. So the watchdog was chosen by the
thing it watches.

*[ask]* Does that make the board useless?

Let them argue before the second bullet. Both sides are respectable: a board
with reputational exposure behaves differently from no board at all, against the
view that structural dependence beats good intentions every time.

*[reveal the second bullet]*

And that is the paper's question, in the specific form it tests it: does board
size and board independence show up in what the fund does - its sustainability
score and its financial performance.
:::

## 3 · Muñoz (2020), boards of socially responsible mutual funds {.smaller}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### The four questions

Come with an answer to each. I will ask.

1.  What are **socially responsible mutual funds**?
2.  What is the **role of the board of trustees**?
3.  Which **indicator measures sustainability**?
4.  What **strategies** incorporate non-financial issues into investment?

### How to prepare

-   On question 1, the definition is easy; the difficulty is that the criteria
    are **chosen by the fund**, which is the same problem green bonds had.
-   On question 2, separate the board's **formal powers** from its **actual
    independence**. Size and independence are what the paper tests.
-   On question 3, ask who produces the score and who pays them.
-   On question 4, the strategies differ enormously in how much they constrain a
    manager. Rank them.

:::

::: notes
This is assessed, so protect the time and do not let the institutions sections
eat it. Run it as a discussion - if you are talking for more than two minutes at
a stretch, stop.

Structure: ten minutes in pairs on questions one and four, then open the floor
on two, then close on three.

*[question 1]*

Funds that apply non-financial criteria - environmental, social, governance -
alongside financial ones when selecting holdings. Then push: who writes the
criteria? The fund does. They met this exact structure with green bonds in
session four, so make them say the parallel out loud rather than saying it
yourself.

*[question 2]*

The oversight body. It hires and can dismiss the investment advisor, approves
fees, and is meant to act for shareholders rather than for the management
company. Size and independence are the two features the paper tests.

*[question 3]*

A sustainability or ESG score assigned to the fund, built up from ratings of the
holdings - Morningstar's globe rating is the usual one in this literature. Then
the question that matters: the rater is paid by whom, and rates what?

*[question 4]*

Negative or exclusionary screening; positive or best-in-class screening;
norms-based screening; ESG integration into valuation; engagement and voting;
impact investing. Make them rank these by how much each actually binds the
manager. Exclusion binds; integration barely does.

*[a caution for you, not for them]*

These are framing notes rather than the paper's findings - check them against
your own reading before class.

*[the connection worth making explicit at the close]*

A mutual fund is how most people will ever hold the portfolio we spent last
session constructing. So who governs the fund is not a side issue; it is the
only governance most investors will ever have.
:::

# 4 · Insurance companies {.divider .center background-color="#06302F"}

## 4 · The principle and the organisational forms

**The principle.** Insurers assume their clients' risk in return for a fee, the
premium. People buy insurance because they are **risk-averse** — they will pay
more than the expected loss to be rid of the variance.

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Stock company** — owned by shareholders, with a profit motive.

**Mutual company** — owned by the policyholders, aiming to provide insurance at
the lowest cost.

**Types.** Life · health · property · credit default swaps · pension plans.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Life insurer asset allocation** (2011)

| Asset | Share |
|:---------------------|------:|
| Bonds | 52.4% |
| Stocks | 28.1% |
| Miscellaneous | 10.4% |
| Loans and mortgages | 9.1% |
:::
::::

::: notes
The principle is one sentence and it is worth making them state it precisely.

*[ask]* If the premium is more than the expected loss, why does anyone buy?

Because they are risk-averse. The premium exceeds the expected payout - it has
to, or the insurer could not exist - and people pay it anyway to remove the
variance. That is the definition of risk aversion with money attached, and it is
the same preference that drove the whole of last session.

*[the two forms]*

Stock company: shareholders, profit motive. Mutual: owned by the policyholders,
so in principle no conflict between insurer and insured. Note that this is the
second time in one session that ownership structure has been offered as a
solution to a conflict of interest - the first was the mutual fund board. Hold
that thought until section seven.

*[the asset table]*

Over half in bonds.

*[ask]* Why bonds rather than equities, when equities return more?

Because the liabilities are long-dated and fairly predictable. An insurer knows
roughly when it will pay and how much, so it buys assets that pay then. That is
duration matching, and it is the opposite of the maturity mismatch a bank runs.
:::

:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="beamer"}

**In the normal course.** Bank A lends €10m to Company C for five years, and
pays an annual premium to Bank B.

**If the credit event occurs.** The defaulted debt transfers to Bank B, Bank B
pays Bank A €10 million, and Bank B recovers what it can from Company C.

The loan never moves; only the credit risk does.

:::

::: notes
Walk the picture rather than defining the instrument first. Definitions land
badly here; the flow does not.

*[the top row]*

Bank A lends ten million to Company C for five years. Ordinary lending. Then
Bank A pays an annual premium to Bank B. Nothing else happens.

*[ask]* What has Bank A bought?

Insurance on the loan.

*[the bottom row]*

Company C defaults. The debt transfers to Bank B, Bank B pays Bank A the ten
million, and Bank B is left to recover whatever it can from Company C.

*[the point, and say it slowly]*

The loan never moved. Bank A still made it and still holds the relationship. All
that moved is the credit risk. That is the whole invention.

*[then the part that matters for 2007]*

A CDS is insurance in everything but name - and it is not called insurance,
which means it was not regulated as insurance.

*[ask]* With fire insurance, what do you need in order to buy a policy?

You have to own the house. With a credit default swap, you do not. You can buy
protection on a loan you did not make, which is not insurance at all - it is a
bet on someone else's default, and there is no limit to how many people can
place it on the same loan. That is why the exposures in 2007 were so much larger
than the debts underneath them.
:::

# 5 · Investment firms {.divider .center background-color="#06302F"}

## 5 · Investment banks

**What they do**

-   **Underwrite** the initial sale of stocks and bonds
-   Make deals in **mergers, acquisitions and spin-offs**
-   Act as **middleman** in the buying and selling of companies
-   **Broker privately** for the very wealthy

::: {.smaller}
**Context.** The line between investment and commercial banking has blurred
again, since legal separation is no longer required.
:::

::: notes
Four activities, and the first one is the one everything else grew out of.

Underwriting is the core: bringing a security to market for the first time.
Everything else - the deal-making, the private brokerage - is the same
relationship sold again.

*[on the context line]*

Worth thirty seconds of history. The separation of investment and commercial
banking was a response to the 1930s, on the view that a bank should not both
hold deposits and underwrite securities. That separation was removed. Whether
the removal mattered is argued about to this day, and it is the backdrop to
every conflict of interest in section seven.

Do not run the argument now. Plant it.
:::

## 5 · Underwriting

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Advice and filing

**Advice.** On market conditions and which security to offer; on when to issue,
how many, and at what price — critical for an IPO.

**Filing.** SEC registration is required for issues above **$1.5 million** with
maturity over **270 days**. The prospectus is made public. Debt issues also need
a credit rating and counsel.

### Firm commitment

The banker **buys the entire offering** at a fixed price and resells it. A
**syndicate** may be formed to spread the underwriting risk. A **tombstone** is
placed in the financial press.

**Three outcomes**

-   **Fully subscribed** — all shares spoken for
-   **Undersubscribed** — the syndicate could not generate interest in all of
    them
-   **Oversubscribed** — more interest than shares, which may lead to rationing

### Alternatives

**Best efforts.** The underwriter does not buy the issue, but makes its best
effort to sell it.

**Private placement.** The entire issue goes to a small, select group — rarely
with equity.

**Equity sales.** Selling a whole division or company: value it, find buyers,
develop confidential financial statements, prepare a letter of intent, assist
with due diligence, reach a definitive agreement.

:::

::: notes
The examinable content is in the second tab. Move through the first and third.

*[tab two - firm commitment, and this is the one to drill]*

Firm commitment means the bank buys the whole issue at a fixed price and then
resells it.

*[ask]* Who carries the risk that nobody wants the shares?

The bank. It has already paid. That is why the syndicate exists - not to raise
more money, but to spread that risk across several banks.

*[the three outcomes]*

Now the question that makes the pricing problem real.

*[ask]* The issue is oversubscribed and the price jumps thirty percent on day
one. Did the bank do a good job?

Let them fight about it. The issuer sold too cheaply and left money on the
table; the bank's buying clients did very well out of it. Oversubscription is
not obviously a success, and whose success it is depends on who the bank was
working for. That is the conflict of interest in section seven, arriving early.

*[tab three]*

Best efforts shifts the risk back to the issuer. Private placement avoids the
registration burden by never going public. Name them and move.
:::

## 5 · Brokers and dealers

:::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
**Order types**

-   **Market order** — buy or sell at the current price
-   **Limit order** — you specify the most you will pay or the least you will
    accept
-   **Short sale** — sell a security you do not own, intending to repurchase it
    later at a lower price

**Brokers.** Full service: research and advice, higher commission. Discount:
execution only.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
**Dealers** hold inventory on their own account and stand ready to buy or sell
— **market makers**, and especially important for thinly traded securities.

**Other services.** Insurance against loss of security documents; **margin
credit** for buying equity with borrowed funds.
:::
::::

::: notes
*[cuttable - they met brokers and dealers in session 3; this is revision]*

If you are running late this is the slide to drop. If you keep it, keep it to
two points.

*[the broker-dealer distinction, which is the one they confuse]*

A broker acts for you and takes a commission. A dealer trades against you from
its own book and makes the spread. Different business, different incentive. They
met this in session three with auction and dealer markets - this is the same
distinction from the firm's side.

*[the short sale, if anyone looks puzzled]*

You borrow the security, sell it, and buy it back later to return it. The loss
is unbounded, which is the only thing about it worth remembering at this stage.
:::

## 5 · Private equity and venture capital

:::: columns
::: {.column width="54%"}
**What it is.** A limited partnership raises funds to invest in new companies or
to buy out existing divisions. The common types are **venture funds** and
**capital buyouts**. The sector expanded after **1978**, when pension funds were
permitted to invest.

**Venture capital firms** provide funds for start-ups and often become closely
involved in management, supplying expertise as well as money.
:::

::: {.column width="46%"}
**Structure.** Mostly limited partnerships, funded by wealthy individuals,
pension funds and corporations, whose investors must wait years before
withdrawing.

**Returns**, 20-year average

| Stage | Return |
|:-------------|-------:|
| Seed | 20.4% |
| All stages | 16.5% |
| Later stage | 13.9% |
:::
::::

::: notes
*[cuttable - the returns table is the droppable half]*

Two things, and the second is the interesting one.

*[the structure]*

Locked up for years. That is not a defect, it is the product: you cannot fund a
company that needs seven years to work with money that can leave in a month. The
illiquidity is what makes the investment possible.

*[the returns - if you keep the table]*

*[ask]* Seed investing returns the most and later-stage the least. Why would
anyone do later-stage?

Because the returns are not risk-adjusted. Seed pays more because most seed
investments are worth nothing. Hold them to the discipline from last session:
a mean return without a standard deviation beside it is not a performance
number. They made exactly this mistake with Hong Kong, and here is the same
trap wearing different clothes.

*[the note the textbook adds, worth being honest about]*

These averages are flattered by exceptional years such as 1999, and the recent
record is much worse. Averages over twenty years hide that.

*[the link to venture capital as a solution, which pays off later]*

One sentence to plant: a venture capitalist sits on the board and is closely
involved in management. Remember that in section seven, when we ask how anyone
solves the principal-agent problem.
:::

# 6 · Bank management {.divider .center background-color="#06302F"}

## 6 · Asset transformation

A bank takes **savings deposits** and uses the funds to make **loans** —
borrowing short and lending long. This is the **maturity mismatch** that has
appeared in every session so far.

:::: columns
::: {.column width="46%"}
**The basic T-account.** A $100 deposit with a 10% reserve requirement:

| Assets | | Liabilities | |
|:---------|-----:|:------------|-----:|
| Reserves | +10 | Deposits | +100 |
| Loans | +90 | | |
:::

::: {.column width="54%"}
**Four concerns**, taken in turn:

1.  **Liquidity** management
2.  **Asset** management
3.  **Liability** management
4.  **Capital adequacy**
:::
::::

::: notes
Asset transformation is the phrase to get them using. A bank turns one kind of
claim into another: short, safe, liquid deposits on one side; long, risky,
illiquid loans on the other.

*[ask]* Who wants to lend for twenty years at a fixed rate? And who wants their
money available on Saturday?

Nobody is the same person. The bank stands between two sets of preferences that
cannot meet directly, and it is paid for standing there. That is the whole
business, and it is the maturity mismatch they have met in every session since
the first.

*[the T-account]*

Deposit of a hundred. Ten percent must be held as reserves, so ten in reserves
and ninety out as loans. Draw it on the board rather than reading it.

*[then the four concerns]*

Say that each of the next four slides is a different way this arrangement can
kill you: you run out of cash, you lend to the wrong people, your funding
disappears, or you have too thin a cushion when losses arrive.
:::

## 6 · Liquidity management

::: ask
Two banks, each facing a **$10 million deposit outflow**.

| | Reserves | Loans | Securities | Deposits | Capital |
|:--------|------:|-----:|------:|------:|-----:|
| **Bank 1** | 20 | 80 | 10 | 100 | 10 |
| **Bank 2** | 10 | 90 | 10 | 100 | 10 |

The reserve requirement is **10%**.

1.  What must each bank do after the outflow?
2.  What are the ways to fill a shortfall, and what does each cost?
:::

::: notes
Five minutes in pairs. This one rewards drawing the T-account, so make them
draw it.

*[bank 1 - excess reserves]*

Reserves fall from twenty to ten, deposits from a hundred to ninety. The
requirement is ten percent of ninety, which is nine. They hold ten.

Nothing needs to happen anywhere. No asset is sold, no loan is called, nobody is
telephoned.

*[bank 2 - no excess reserves]*

Reserves fall from ten to zero, deposits to ninety. The requirement is nine.
They hold nothing.

A nine million shortfall, and it has to be filled today.

*[part two - the four remedies, and the cost of each]*

Sell securities - you give up their return. Borrow from other banks or
corporations - you pay interest, and the rate is highest exactly when everyone
needs it. Borrow from the central bank - cheaper, but there may be a stigma to
being seen there. Call in or sell off loans - the most expensive of all, because
you destroy the customer relationship that was the point of making the loan.

*[the lesson, and this is the sentence to get them to write]*

Excess reserves are insurance against deposit outflows, and the premium is the
return the bank gives up by holding them. Bank 1 paid that premium. Bank 2 saved
it and is now making phone calls.

**Worked.** Bank 1: reserves 10 against deposits 90, requirement 9 - no action
needed. Bank 2: reserves 0 against deposits 90, a $9m shortfall, filled by
selling securities, borrowing from banks or the central bank, or calling in
loans - each with a cost.
:::

## 6 · Asset and liability management

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Asset management.** Earn the highest return on assets while minimising risk:
find borrowers with low default risk paying high rates; buy securities with high
return and low risk; diversify; and manage liquidity.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Liability management.** Manage the **sources** of funds — deposits,
certificates of deposit, other debt.

Important since the **1960s**: banks no longer depend primarily on deposits, and
when they see loan opportunities they borrow or issue CDs to fund them.
:::
::::

::: keyidea
Both sides are now managed **jointly**, through an asset–liability committee —
which is why CDs and borrowing have displaced checkable deposits over recent
decades.
:::

::: notes
The content here is thin; the change over time is the interesting part, so lead
with that.

Asset management is the obvious half: lend well, invest well, diversify, stay
liquid.

*[liability management - this is the shift worth explaining]*

Until the 1960s, the liability side was not managed at all. Deposits arrived or
they did not, and the bank lent whatever showed up. Funding was a constraint,
not a choice.

Then banks discovered they could go and buy funding - issue a certificate of
deposit, borrow in the interbank market - which reverses the logic entirely. You
find the loan first and fund it afterwards.

*[ask]* What does that change about how risky a bank is?

Growth is no longer limited by how much the public wants to deposit. A bank can
expand as fast as someone will lend to it, and wholesale funding leaves far
faster than retail deposits when confidence goes. Every bank that failed quickly
in 2008 was funded this way.
:::

## 6 · Capital adequacy

::: ask
Two banks, each with **reserves 10** and **loans 90**.

| | Deposits | Capital |
|:-----------------------|------:|-----:|
| **High capital bank** | 90 | 10 |
| **Low capital bank** | 96 | 4 |

Both now suffer a **$5 million loan loss**.

1.  What happens to each?
2.  Why, then, would any bank hold **low** capital?
:::

::: notes
This is the most important slide in the section. Three minutes in pairs, then
board work.

*[part one - do it as a T-account, not as a sentence]*

Loans fall from ninety to eighty-five in both banks. The loss has to land
somewhere, and it lands on capital, because capital is what absorbs losses
before depositors do.

High capital bank: capital ten, less five, equals five. Still solvent.

Low capital bank: capital four, less five, equals minus one. Insolvent. Assets
are worth less than what it owes.

Same loss. Same loans. One bank survives and the other does not, and the only
difference was the cushion.

*[part two - the question that makes it interesting]*

*[ask]* So why would any bank hold low capital?

Push them to answer with arithmetic, not with greed.

Return on equity is return on assets times the equity multiplier, where the
multiplier is assets over equity capital. More capital means a bigger
denominator, a smaller multiplier, and a lower return on equity. The same
profit, spread over more equity, is a worse number for shareholders.

So safety and return on equity pull against each other, directly. The low
capital bank is not being reckless by accident - it is maximising the thing its
shareholders are watching. That is why capital requirements are imposed rather
than left to judgement.

**Worked.** A $5m loss leaves the high capital bank with capital of +5, solvent;
the low capital bank at −1, insolvent. Banks hold low capital because
ROE = ROA × EM, so more capital lowers return on equity.
:::

## 6 · Managing the capital position

$$ROE = ROA \times EM \qquad EM = \frac{\text{assets}}{\text{equity capital}}$$

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Too much capital** — raise the multiplier:

-   sell or retire stock
-   raise dividends, reducing retained earnings
-   grow assets by issuing debt such as CDs
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Too little capital** — lower the multiplier:

-   issue stock
-   cut dividends, retaining earnings
-   slow asset growth by retiring debt
:::
::::

::: notes
*[cuttable - the previous slide carries the idea; this is the mechanics]*

Six levers, three each way, and they are mirror images. Do not read all six.

Make one observation and leave it.

*[ask]* Look at the two lists. What happens to a banking system where every bank
is simultaneously told it has too little capital?

They all issue stock at once into a falling market, they all cut dividends, and
they all shrink their assets - which means calling in loans, from businesses, in
the middle of whatever crisis prompted the instruction. Individually prudent and
collectively destructive. That is the argument about procyclical capital
regulation in one question, and it is worth more than the six bullet points.
:::

# 7 · Economic efficiency and asymmetric information {.divider .center background-color="#06302F"}

## Why is almost no finance direct? {.hook background-color="#FAF7F2"}

Firms need money. Savers have money. The obvious arrangement is for savers to
buy the firms' stocks and bonds.

::: incremental
-   **That is not how it works.** Issuing marketable debt and equity is not the
    primary way businesses are financed; indirect finance is many times larger
    than direct, and **banks are the most important source of external funds**.
-   Only large, well-established corporations have easy access to securities
    markets at all.
-   Something prevents the obvious arrangement from working. The remainder of the
    session identifies what.
:::

::: notes
This is the payoff of the whole chapter, so set it up as a puzzle and let it sit
before you resolve it.

State the obvious arrangement first, and make it sound sensible, because it is.
Firms need capital. Households have savings. Stocks and bonds exist precisely to
connect them.

*[reveal the first bullet, and let it land]*

It is not how it works. Direct finance is a small part of the picture. The
dominant route is indirect - through a bank - and that has been true across
countries and across decades.

*[ask]* Why pay a bank to stand in the middle? The bank takes a margin. Going
direct is cheaper.

Let them try. The answers they give will be about convenience or ignorance.

*[reveal the second bullet]*

Then narrow it. It is not that nobody uses securities markets - it is that only
large, established firms can. Size is the thing that predicts access.

*[ask]* What do large firms have that small ones do not, apart from money?

A reputation. A public record. Audited accounts going back years. People know
what they are.

That is information, and the rest of the section is about what happens when it
is missing.
:::

## 7 · Facts about financial structure

::: incremental
-   **Stocks are not the main source of external finance.** Indirect finance is
    many times more important than direct, and banks are the most important
    source of external funds.
-   **The system is heavily regulated**, and only large, well-established
    corporations have easy access to securities markets.
-   **Collateral is prevalent** in debt contracts, for households and businesses
    alike, and debt contracts are complicated legal documents placing
    substantial restrictions on borrowers.
-   **Transactions costs** hinder the flow of funds to people with productive
    investment opportunities, and leave small investors unable to diversify.
:::

::: {.source}
Intermediaries profit by reducing those costs — economies of scale, as with
mutual funds, and developed expertise.
:::

::: notes
Four facts, revealed one at a time, and each one is a clue. Tell them that:
these are the observations any theory of financial structure has to explain.

*[fact one]* Banks dominate. Already established on the hook slide.

*[fact two]* Heavy regulation, and access restricted to the large and
well-known.

*[fact three - the one they underrate]*

Collateral everywhere, and contracts full of restrictions. Ask why a lender
would want a covenant that stops a borrower doing things. The answer is coming
in two slides.

*[fact four]*

Transactions costs, and the specific consequence: a small investor cannot
diversify. Last session they built a twelve-market portfolio. With two thousand
euros you cannot.

*[the source line]*

Which is the first answer to the chapter's question. The intermediary exists
because it has economies of scale and expertise that an individual cannot have.

Then say plainly: that is a real answer and it is not sufficient. Transactions
costs do not explain why collateral is everywhere or why contracts are so
restrictive. Something else is going on, and it is on the next slide.
:::

## 7 · Asymmetric information: the two problems

**Asymmetric information** — the parties to a transaction do not have the same
information.

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Adverse selection**

Occurs **before** the transaction. One party has better information than the
other about what is being traded.

*Hidden information.*
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Moral hazard**

Occurs **after** the agreement. One party has an incentive to behave differently
once the deal is struck.

*Hidden action.*
:::
::::

::: keyidea
**Agency theory** is the analysis of how these two problems affect behaviour.
The distinction between them is **timing**: before the deal, or after it.
:::

::: notes
This is the distinction they must leave with, and the only reliable way to teach
it is the timing test. Drill the timing, not the definitions.

Before or after. That is the whole thing.

Adverse selection is hidden information before the deal: you cannot tell what
you are buying. Moral hazard is hidden action after it: behaviour changes once
the money has moved.

*[ask]* Insurance. Someone who already knows they are ill buys health cover -
which is it?

Adverse selection. The information existed before the contract.

*[ask]* And someone who takes up smoking because they now have health cover?

Moral hazard. The behaviour changed after it.

Run two or three more of these out loud. It takes two minutes and it is worth
more than any definition, because the minicases at the end of the session are
exactly this test, and so is the exam question.
:::

## 7 · Adverse selection: the lemons problem

::: {.content-visible unless-format="beamer"}

```{=html}
<div class="lemons">
<svg viewBox="0 0 1440 400" role="img" aria-labelledby="lemT lemD"
     style="width:100%;height:auto;max-height:380px;display:block;margin:0 auto;font-family:inherit" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet">
<title id="lemT">The lemons problem in securities markets</title>
<desc id="lemD">Buyers who cannot tell good securities from bad pay the average value. Good issuers, underpaid, withdraw; bad issuers, overpaid, issue more. The mix worsens, the average falls, and the argument repeats until the market thins out.</desc>

</defs>

<line x1="325.0" y1="223" x2="325.0" y2="241" stroke="#40607D" stroke-width="2"/>

<line x1="1135.0" y1="223" x2="1135.0" y2="241" stroke="#40607D" stroke-width="2"/>
<text class="dg-lab" x="1135.0" y="264" fill="#40607D">a good security, worth 100</text>
<circle cx="730.0" cy="232" r="8" fill="#B4573C"/>
<text class="dg-labc" x="730.0" y="210">buyers pay the average, 70</text>
<line x1="1135.0" y1="222" x2="1135.0" y2="172" stroke="#63716E" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 3"/>
<path class="dg-arr" d="M1135.0 172 L757.0 172" marker-end="url(#ahc)"/>
<text class="dg-lab" x="946.0" y="158" fill="#40607D">paid 70 for something worth 100 — the good issuer withdraws</text>
<line x1="325.0" y1="276" x2="325.0" y2="300" stroke="#63716E" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 3"/>
<path class="dg-arr" d="M325.0 300 L703.0 300" marker-end="url(#ahc)"/>
<text class="dg-lab" x="514.0" y="322" fill="#40607D">paid 70 for something worth 40 — the bad issuer sells more</text>
<text class="dg-note" x="40" y="382">The remaining mix worsens, the average falls, and further good issuers withdraw. Buyers anticipate this and withdraw their bids.</text>
</svg>

```

:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="beamer"}

A buyer who cannot tell a good security (worth 100) from a bad one (worth 40)
pays the average, 70. The good issuer, paid 70 for something worth 100,
withdraws. The bad issuer, paid 70 for something worth 40, sells more. The mix
worsens, the average falls, and buyers anticipate all of it and stop bidding.

:::

::: {.smaller}
**Where it bites least.** Well-known firms have less asymmetric information, so
a smaller lemons problem — which is why large firms can use direct finance and
small ones cannot.
:::

::: notes
Use the picture and walk it left to right; the argument is a sequence, not a
state.

*[set it up]*

A buyer faces two kinds of security and cannot tell them apart. Good ones are
worth a hundred, bad ones forty.

*[ask]* What will they pay?

Something in between. Call it seventy - the average, weighted by how many of
each they think are out there.

*[now the two arrows]*

Look what that price does to each issuer.

The good issuer is offered seventy for something worth a hundred. They withdraw.
Why would they sell at a thirty percent discount?

The bad issuer is offered seventy for something worth forty. They issue as much
as they can.

*[the loop - this is the part that makes it a mechanism rather than an anecdote]*

So the mix left in the market gets worse. Which means the average falls. Which
drives out the next tier of good issuers. And buyers, who are not stupid, work
all of this out in advance and decline to bid at all.

The market does not clear badly. It can fail to exist.

*[then the payoff line, pointing at the smaller text]*

And now the fact from the hook slide is explained. Large well-known firms have
less asymmetric information, so a smaller lemons problem, so they can sell
securities directly. Small firms cannot, and go to a bank instead.

*[ask]* Why does the bank not have the same problem?

Hold the question - it is the next slide.
:::

## 7 · Four solutions to adverse selection

::: incremental
1.  **Private production and sale of information** — undermined by the
    **free-rider problem**: whoever pays for the research cannot stop others
    acting on it.
2.  **Government regulation to increase information** — mandatory audits,
    disclosure requirements.
3.  **Financial intermediation** — a bank makes **private** loans, so nobody
    free-rides on what it learns; the used-car dealer is the standard analogy.
4.  **Collateral and net worth** — which reduce the consequence of the problem:
    the lender is protected whether or not the borrower proves to be a lemon.
:::

::: notes
Four solutions, revealed one at a time, and the third is the answer to the
chapter's question.

*[one]*

Sell information to investors. Then the objection: if you buy my research and
act on it, the price moves, and everyone who did not pay observes the price and
free-rides. The information business is hard to do well for exactly this reason.

*[two]*

Make firms disclose. Audits, filings, prospectuses. It helps and it does not
eliminate the problem - firms still choose how to present what they disclose.

*[three - stop here and make it land]*

The bank's loans are private. It learns about the borrower and nobody else gets
to use what it learns, because the loan is not traded. The free-rider problem
simply does not arise.

*[ask]* So what is a bank, in one sentence?

An institution that profits from producing information about borrowers that
nobody else can copy. The used-car dealer is the same business: it knows which
cars are lemons, it buys and resells on its own account, and its reputation is
the asset.

That is the answer to the question this chapter opened with. Say it as the
answer: the intermediary exists because information is expensive to produce and
impossible to keep once it is public.

*[four]*

Collateral and net worth make the whole question less urgent. If the loan is
secured, the lender's downside is covered whether or not the borrower turned out
to be a lemon. And now fact three from two slides ago - collateral is everywhere
- is explained rather than merely observed.
:::

## 7 · Moral hazard

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**In equity — the principal-agent problem**

Ownership by stockholders is separated from control by managers, and managers
may act in their own interest rather than the owners'.

*Solutions:* monitoring; government regulation to increase information;
financial intermediation such as **venture capital**; and using **debt**
contracts instead.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**In debt**

Debt creates an incentive to take on **very risky projects**: the upside accrues
to the borrower, while the downside falls partly on the lender.

*Solutions:* net worth and collateral; monitoring and enforcement of
**restrictive covenants**; and financial intermediation, since banks have
special advantages in monitoring.
:::
::::

::: {.source}
**What covenants do.** Discourage undesirable behaviour · encourage desirable
behaviour · keep collateral valuable · provide information.
:::

::: notes
Two forms, and the neat thing is that the cure for one is the cause of the
other. Make sure that lands.

*[equity - the principal-agent problem]*

Owners are not managers. Managers may build empires, take comfortable decisions,
or simply not work very hard, and the owners cannot see which.

*[ask]* You own ten percent of a business and manage it. You can work very hard
and add a hundred thousand of value. How much of that do you get?

Ten thousand. So you work a tenth as hard as the owner of the whole thing would.
Nothing dishonest has happened; the incentive is simply diluted.

Then connect it back: this is why a venture capitalist sits on the board and
involves themselves in management. It is monitoring, bought at the price of the
investor's own time.

*[debt]*

Now the fix. Give the firm debt instead of equity and the manager keeps the
whole upside, so the incentive is restored.

*[ask]* What have we just created?

The opposite problem. With debt, the borrower keeps all the gain above the
repayment and the lender eats the loss below it. So the borrower wants risk -
the riskier the better, once things are tight. This is minicase two, and it is
also every bank in 2008.

*[covenants]*

Which is why debt contracts are not one line long. Covenants stop the borrower
doing the things the contract made attractive. And fact three from three slides
ago - contracts are complicated legal documents with substantial restrictions -
is now explained too.
:::

## 7 · Conflicts of interest

A **type of moral hazard**: a person or institution has multiple interests, and
serving one is detrimental to another.

::: incremental
-   **Underwriting and research** in investment banking. The bank researches
    companies and underwrites their securities. Research is supposed to be
    unbiased — yet underwriting is easier when research is positive.
-   **Auditing and consulting** in accounting firms. The auditor gives an
    unbiased opinion on financial health while the consulting arm earns fees from
    the same client — especially compromising when consulting fees exceed audit
    fees.
-   **Credit assessment and consulting** in rating agencies. The same structure:
    rating a security while being paid to advise the issuer.
:::

::: notes
Lead with the classification, because it is the thing they get wrong in the
exam: a conflict of interest is a species of moral hazard, not a third category
beside it.

The structure is identical in all three cases, so say the structure once and
then let the three examples be variations.

One institution, two jobs, and doing the second one well makes the first one
worse.

*[the three, revealed one at a time]*

Research and underwriting. Audit and consulting. Rating and advising.

*[ask]* In each case, who is paying, and who is relying on the output?

That is the whole diagnosis. The issuer pays; the public relies. Every time
those two are different people, the conflict is structural rather than personal.

*[and the honest complication, if the room is good]*

Ask why we do not simply ban the combinations. Because the information is cheaper
to produce when one firm does both - the analyst who researches a company
understands it well enough to bring it to market. The synergy is real. That is
what makes this a genuine problem rather than an obvious one.
:::

## 7 · Identifying the problem: six cases

::: ask
For each, name the problem — **adverse selection**, **moral hazard**, or a
**conflict of interest** — and say **why**.

1.  Rating agencies help structure debt so that it attains high ratings.
2.  A firm owes $100 in interest, has $90, and starts looking for risky projects.
3.  An Apple lawyer trades on confidential earnings information.
4.  A silent partner funds 90%; Steve manages the business and goes to the beach.
5.  Enron hides its problems; Arthur Andersen pleads guilty.
6.  Tech-boom research is distorted to please issuers.
:::

::: notes
Ten minutes in pairs, then take them one by one. Make them say "before" or
"after" before they name the category.

One. Conflict of interest. The agency rates and consults for the same issuer,
and the fees compromise the rating.

Two. Moral hazard in debt. The firm has nothing left to lose, so the incentive
is to gamble with the lender's money. Ninety against a hundred owed - a safe
project leaves them bankrupt anyway, so only a risky one can save them, and the
lender pays for the attempt.

Three. Adverse selection. One party to the trade has better information than the
other about what is being traded. Note it is also illegal, but the category is
adverse selection.

Four. Moral hazard in equity - the principal-agent problem. Steve keeps only
five thousand of every hundred thousand of value he creates, so he does not
create it.

Five. Conflict of interest. The auditor was also a paid consultant to the firm
it audited.

Six. Conflict of interest. Research and underwriting in the same bank;
favourable coverage bought banking business.

*[the distinction to drill, and close the session on it]*

Before or after. Adverse selection is hidden information before the deal - you
cannot tell what you are buying. Moral hazard is hidden action after it -
behaviour changes once the money has changed hands.

Minicase three is before. Two and four are after. And conflicts of interest are
a species of moral hazard, not a third category - which is the single most
common error in the exam.

**Worked.** 1 conflict of interest · 2 moral hazard in debt · 3 adverse
selection · 4 principal-agent · 5 conflict of interest · 6 conflict of interest.
:::
